Von Willebrand disease (type 1) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and frequently manifests with mucosal bleeding (gingival, epistaxis) and bruising; it is often underdiagnosed and may only become clinically apparent after hemostatic challenges like extractions. Hemophilia A is less likely in females but cannot be excluded without sex and family history—though spontaneous bruising is atypical, post-procedural bleeding can be severe, especially if factor VIII levels are <5%. Acquired von Willebrand syndrome is associated with lymphoproliferative disorders, autoimmune conditions, or cardiovascular disease (e.g., aortic stenosis), and may present de novo with mucosal bleeding in adults. Myelodysplastic syndrome is lower probability in absence of cytopenias beyond platelets, fatigue, or abnormal CBC—but age-agnostic consideration is warranted given clonal hematopoiesis risk and potential for isolated thrombocytopenia with dysplastic megakaryocytes.
